title: A language of 690 roots in eleven fields of meaning, inflected, in two registers, written page by page about what each part of the book pictures
method:
THE LANGUAGE WAS DESIGNED BEFORE ANY TEXT WAS WRITTEN, and the text is then written in it.

Script. The author invents a language, not a script: he writes in the script his book is written in (EVA-basic, 31 strokes). The shapes his roots take, the way an ending continues a stem, and the stroke a word takes at a line end are drawn from the habits of that writing, fitted on the 192 public training pages. The 34 pages the practice evaluation scores were never fitted on and the hidden held-out pages were never read.

Lexicon. 690 roots in eleven fields of meaning -- plants, parts of plants, water, rooms, stars, sky, body, time, making, drugs, and a general field -- 60 roots in each field and 90 in the general one. A root is a shape his script holds, made once and kept.

Grammar. A stem may carry a leading syllable out of fifteen prefixes, and an ending of nought to three strokes. The ending is not bolted on: the pen goes on from the end of the stem as the habits of the script lead it, and stops where a word stops, so the form is part of the stem's own shape. How far the pen goes is the form and the form is the case. A closed class of forty-one particles carries connection, demonstration and negation, and stands for a quarter of the words. A sentence is one to eight words; three sentences in ten take a final particle. A word is repeated in another form 14 times in a hundred -- another ending, one stroke changed, the stroke drawn from the pen's habit at that place -- and a word already on the page is taken up again 30 times in a hundred.

Two registers, A and B, differ by fixed correspondences at the edges of a word: final -l becomes -m, -aiin becomes -ain, initial q becomes k. A page is written in the register the codicological record gives it.

Subject. A page is written about what the pictures of that part of the book are about: the herbal draws on plants and their parts, the balneological pages on rooms and water, the astronomical pages on stars, sky and time, the pharmacological pages on drugs, the recipes on making and time, with the general field underneath. A paragraph opens with a title formula, a heading word out of a closed set of ten.

The line is written to the margin, as in the book: the width is drawn from the fitted distribution of line widths, and when the room left is small a shorter form of the word is taken -- the stem without its prefix, an ending left off. At the line's end the last word takes the closing stroke the hand gives words there.

Spelling drift. At any stroke, once in four, the pen goes where it is used to going rather than where the dictionary has it. This is what makes the text look written rather than assembled; it is also, as it turns out, what costs it the most.

RESULT ON THE PRACTICE EVALUATION: 12 of the 22 established facts. It reproduces F-003 (paragraph-initial p and f, 143 against threshold 10), F-004, F-008, F-009, F-014, F-017, F-018 (words follow the section, 1.30 against the across-page shuffle at p = 0.005), F-019, F-021, F-022, F-023 and F-024.

IT BUYS ONE FACT THAT NO MEANINGLESS PROCEDURE HAS GOT, and pays for it with the glyph-level ones. F-014, two word types in three occurring once: this text gives 0.798 where the manuscript gives 0.711 and the threshold is 0.667. My own meaningless procedure, which reproduces 19 of the 22 (PR #613), gets 0.648 on this fact and cannot get it at any setting that keeps the within-page reuse the manuscript has: a reuse rate and a singleton share are bought with the same coin unless something re-makes the word each time it is used. A lexicon with inflection does exactly that -- the same root comes back in a form that has not been seen -- and the fact falls.

WHAT THE LANGUAGE LOSES, and why. Against the same meaningless procedure it loses F-001 (2.9 against 11.3), F-002 (0.113 against 0.163), F-005, F-006, F-007 (0.070 against 0.202), F-010, F-013 (2.77 against 2.03, against a ceiling of 2.1) and F-016 (0.110 against 0.282). The reason is one thing: a text whose words are looked up in a dictionary does not have the manuscript's glyph-level structure. The manuscript's glyph stream costs 1.94 bits given the two strokes before it; a text built from 690 roots, 15 prefixes and 41 particles, however those shapes were first drawn, re-assembles them in orders the pen was never set for, and the entropy of the result is 2.77. Every fact about how strokes run into strokes across a word boundary -- the edge dependence, its breaking at the line end, the near-copies within the last ten words -- falls with it. To hold those facts the words have to be written by the hand, not chosen from a list; and a language is a list.

WHAT NEITHER APPROACH TOUCHES. F-011 (nearby pages sharing words) and F-020 (pages of one Currier language sharing words) are missed by the meaningless procedure and by this language alike: the registers give same-register pages shared correspondences but not a shared enough vocabulary to beat the label-shuffled and label-rotated nulls (-0.081 here), and pages of a quire drift apart faster than the manuscript's do.

CONTROLS. With the spelling drift off and a smaller lexicon (26 roots a field), F-016 comes back to 0.298 and F-014 falls to 0.684, still above the threshold, while F-013 only comes down to 2.36: shrinking the dictionary buys back the reuse but not the glyph stream. With the word choice sharpened so that the pen only takes up words whose first stroke it is set for, F-013 comes to 2.29 but the title formula collapses to a single word and the repeated three-word runs of F-024 rise from 0.0008 to 0.0189, which is the one setting tried that fails that fact. The two properties -- a tight glyph stream and a working vocabulary -- pull against each other in every setting tried.

GUARDS. 4,487 ordinary lines and 738 paragraph-opening lines, exactly the manuscript's counts; 49,799 tokens; 0 four-word runs of the manuscript; 0 uncertainty markers.

WHAT THIS SHOWS. The step says an invented language earns credit where meaningless procedures fail. It does fail one, F-014, and the mechanism is clear: inflection re-makes a repeated word, which is the only way seen so far to hold a high singleton share and a high within-page reuse at once. But the same property -- words drawn from a fixed inventory -- breaks the tightest structure in the manuscript, the run of the strokes themselves. A constructed language written in this script reproduces what a language is for (words about subjects, forms that repeat with variation) and cannot reproduce what this text does (a glyph stream as tight as a hand's). If the manuscript is a language, it is one whose vocabulary is far smaller and far more stereotyped than any that would carry these 690 roots' worth of meaning; if it is not, the fact that a language fails where a procedure succeeds is the shape of the evidence.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW: that the manuscript is or is not a language. This is one constructed language, designed by one person in one evening, with one set of rates; a different language -- a smaller closed vocabulary, morphology that is a spelling rather than a suffix, dialects defined by vocabulary rather than by sound laws -- might do better on the facts it misses. The claim is only about the trade-off measured above, which held across every setting tried.
